285.bp: Cities generate vast amounts of data—building energy use, traffic patterns, emissions, population movement—and planners want to use that data to understand what happens if they make different choices today. The question is: what future does a particular policy lead to? This matters because once you build a highway or zone land, changing it is expensive and slow.
285.wh: The real problem is that data describing cities is scattered everywhere: some lives in building management systems, some in traffic sensors, some in satellite images, and some exists only in spreadsheets and government offices. These sources disagree on definitions, they update at different speeds, and they don't talk to each other. A road network dataset might be three years old while real traffic has changed. A forecast tool might expect inputs in one format but receive them in another. Tying all of it together to ask 'what if' questions is like trying to assemble a jigsaw puzzle where some pieces are missing and others don't match.
285.ap: This paper argues for treating scenario-building as a serious problem in itself: not as a technical algorithm, but as a systems challenge that touches digital twins (digital copies of the city), GIS (geographic information systems), simulations, forecasting tools, and the organizational workflows that actually run planning meetings. The authors map out where the temporal mismatches occur—data quality gaps, versions that fall out of sync, integrations that break when one system updates—and propose thinking of urban planning as a data continuity problem, not just a calculation problem.
285.ww: The insight is that you cannot answer a 'what if' question reliably unless your input data is consistent, current, and understood the same way by every tool using it. A climate scenario built on 2023 building data but 2021 traffic data is nonsensical—you don't know which trends are real and which are artifacts of stale information. By focusing on the temporal and definitional coherence of data pipelines rather than jumping straight to forecasting, the paper makes visible the invisible work that has to happen first.
285.po: The payoff is a diagnostic framework: cities can now ask, for each layer of their planning infrastructure (GIS, simulation, forecasting, decision-support systems), 'which temporal and integration gaps block us from running reliable scenarios?' This reframes the work from 'build a better model' to 'make our existing data trustworthy enough to support scenario-building,' which is often cheaper and faster.

286.bp: Fake news spreads quickly and damages public trust. Automated detection—software that can flag false news before it spreads—is a valuable defense, but only if the detector actually works in the real messy world where bad actors are actively trying to fool it.
286.wh: Researchers have noticed that certain emotions and sentiments appear more often in false news: outrage, fear, strong partisan language. So detection systems learn to flag articles that feel emotional as likely to be false. But this creates a vulnerability: an adversary with a large language model can rewrite a false article to sound calm and neutral, stripping out the emotional language but keeping the lies intact. The detector gets fooled because it relied on the emotional signal as a shortcut, not on actual truth or the substance of claims.
286.ap: This paper introduces AdSent, a framework that takes this vulnerability seriously. First, they use a language model to generate adversarial versions of news—taking false articles and rewriting them in different emotional tones while keeping the lies intact. Second, they measure how much existing detectors break when sentiment changes. Third, they build a new detector designed to make consistent predictions regardless of whether an article sounds emotional or calm, by learning to ignore sentiment shifts and focus on deeper patterns.
286.ww: The mechanism works because a detector that explicitly learns 'this prediction should be the same whether the article is angry or calm' is forced to find other reasons for the prediction beyond the emotional tone. It has to latch onto actual inconsistencies in the story, claims that contradict known facts, or structural patterns of misinformation that remain even when the tone changes. By making sentiment irrelevant, the detector has to work harder and rely on more robust signals.
286.po: The result is a detector that remains accurate even when an adversary rewrites the article to sound different. Testing shows that models trained this way keep their accuracy when sentiment is manipulated, whereas traditional detectors often flip their predictions. This is concrete progress toward detection that works against adaptive adversaries, not just against naive false news.

287.bp: Three-dimensional point cloud data—millions of tiny (x, y, z) coordinates that represent physical objects and scenes—is becoming central to robotics, autonomous vehicles, and 3D sensing. But these systems can be attacked: small changes to the point cloud, imperceptible to a human viewer, can fool the AI into misclassifying what it sees.
287.wh: Defending against these attacks is hard. If you modify the model itself (adding defensive layers, retraining), you're invasive—the model becomes proprietary and slow. If you try to filter or clean the point cloud, you need training data specific to the attack, or you need to know what the attack looks like in advance. What you really want is a lightweight, universal shield that works after the model is built, requires no extra training, and stops the attack without harming normal performance.
287.ap: This paper proposes PWAVEP, which works in the spectral domain—a mathematical space where the point cloud is represented not as individual points but as frequencies, like a sound decomposed into bass, midrange, and treble. The key insight is that adversarial attacks hide in the high-frequency components (the 'noise-like' parts of the spectrum). PWAVEP computes a score for each point based on how salient and sparse it is in this spectral view, then removes the most salient points (identified as adversarial outliers) and filters the high-frequency parts for moderately salient points, using a mathematical tool called graph wavelet transforms.
287.ww: The reason this works is physical: imperceptible attacks are typically designed to look like noise, so they concentrate in high-frequency components. By selectively suppressing those frequencies, you remove the attack while preserving the structure of the actual object. Removing the most severely corrupted points is conservative but effective—you lose a few real points but eliminate the attack entirely. The method requires no knowledge of what attack was used; it works generally because all imperceptible attacks share the property of living in high-frequency space.
287.po: PWAVEP is plug-and-play and non-invasive: you can apply it to any model without retraining, without auxiliary data, without modifying the model's weights. Testing shows it achieves higher accuracy and robustness than existing defenses, meaning it stops attacks effectively while keeping the model's accuracy on clean data intact. This makes it practical to deploy as a defense layer in real-world 3D sensing systems.

288.bp: The web is changing from a system where humans read documents to one where AI agents autonomously browse websites, gather information, make decisions, and act on behalf of users or services. This shift could unlock tremendous automation, but it also threatens the economic and legal foundations of the web as it exists today.
288.wh: The tension is this: when agents crawl websites to serve user requests, they consume bandwidth and content without paying for it. They also don't respect the business models that websites depend on—a news site that makes money selling ads to humans sees no revenue when an agent scrapes its articles and serves them to another audience. There are no agreed standards for which agents can access what, no way to enforce permissions at scale, and legal remedies (blocking agents, suing) are slow and antagonistic. Meanwhile, the Global South is less represented in tech governance, so their concerns—about data extraction, sovereignty, labor impacts—often don't shape the rules being written.
288.ap: This paper reports on a workshop in Brazil with representatives from tech companies, media, government, and academia to examine these tensions from the perspective of countries in the Global South. The authors map three core misalignments: first, there's no standardized way to tell agents 'don't access this content'; second, agent-driven content consumption (an agent reading and summarizing news instead of ads being shown) breaks ad-based business models; third, governance mechanisms that exist in rich countries don't apply globally, creating extractive dynamics where data flows one direction.
288.ww: The insight is that the problem isn't technical—it's economic and political. Standards and blocking rules are only effective if everyone agrees to follow them, and agreement requires fair incentives and transparent governance. Without that, companies in rich countries can ignore restrictions, while countries with less market power have no leverage. The paper argues that the current responses—broad bot blocking, legal fights—just hide the misalignment rather than solving it.
288.po: The payoff is a reframing: instead of fighting agents with blocking and litigation, the agentic web can be sustainable if it includes transparent standards (everyone knows which agents can access what), inclusive governance (voices from the Global South shape the rules), and incentive rebalancing (agents and websites have mechanisms to negotiate access and payment). This is a blueprint for making the agentic web an open, fair infrastructure rather than a tool for extraction.

289.bp: Artificial intelligence is everywhere: in content moderation, security systems, medical advice, hiring, and criminal justice. This creates a paradox: AI can help defend against misinformation, deepfakes, and attacks, but the same AI tools can also generate lies, create fake evidence, and automate large-scale deception. The question is how to steer AI toward the defensive and away from the destructive.
289.wh: The challenge is that the capabilities are symmetric. The same language model that can help detect misinformation can also generate persuasive falsehoods. The same computer vision system that can identify fake images can be used to create more convincing fakes. Defensive tools are reactive—they have to catch attacks after they happen. Offensive tools are proactive—they can generate new attacks that defenses haven't seen yet. There's also the societal layer: deploying AI at scale without understanding its harms (erosion of trust, privacy violations, manipulation) is risky, but so is being paralyzed by fear and missing the benefits.
289.ap: This is a workshop paper, not a research contribution with a method. It announces the AiOfAi workshop series, which brings together researchers and practitioners to discuss the dual nature of AI—how to amplify its defensive uses (intrusion detection, threat modeling, access control) while constraining its offensive uses. The workshop creates space to examine both the harms (disinformation, privacy breaches, social engineering) and the opportunities (new defense mechanisms, ethical governance, resilience).
289.ww: The reasoning is that understanding happens in dialogue. By bringing security researchers, ethicists, industry practitioners, and policymakers into the same room, the workshop creates visibility into what's actually happening with AI deployed at scale. It acknowledges that there's no single 'solution' but rather a need for ongoing negotiation between innovation, safety, and fairness.
289.po: The concrete outcome is a forum where emerging harms (deepfakes, automated social engineering, erosion of verification) are documented alongside emerging defenses, and ethical and legal frameworks are discussed while the technology is still young enough to be shaped. This is infrastructure for responsible AI development.

290.bp: Doctors use AI to help answer patient questions quickly, but healthcare is high-stakes: a wrong answer can hurt someone. One big source of errors is ambiguous questions. A patient asking 'I have stomach pain, what should I do?' could mean anything from indigestion to appendicitis to anxiety. The AI needs to recognize when a question is underspecified and ask for clarification before answering.
290.wh: The problem is that large language models are confident and fluent—they generate a plausible-sounding answer to nearly any question without signaling doubt or asking for more information. They also have a blindness to their own blindness: they don't know what they don't know. A model fine-tuned to answer medical questions will try to answer ambiguous questions directly, often making reasonable guesses that are sometimes dead wrong. Existing methods that estimate uncertainty typically require retraining the model or running it multiple times, which is slow and expensive in a real medical setting.
290.ap: This paper introduces a new framework grounded in the observation that uncertainty lives in the model's internal states—the numerical patterns in its hidden layers. The authors first build a benchmark of medical questions specifically designed to be ambiguous in clinically relevant ways (CV-MedBench). Then they show that input ambiguity—underspecification of the question—is measurably encoded in the model's internal activations: the model's hidden layers literally represent 'I don't have enough information.' Based on this, they introduce AU-Probe, a small add-on module trained to detect ambiguity directly from these hidden states. When AU-Probe detects ambiguity, the system asks the patient clarifying questions before answering.
290.ww: The mechanism works because neural networks don't just store information sequentially; they build representations that compress what they know and don't know. A well-trained model asked an ambiguous medical question will have activation patterns that reflect the ambiguity itself. By training a small probe to read that signal, you create a lightweight detector that doesn't require retraining the main model, doesn't need multiple forward passes, and works in a single inference step. The clarifying questions push back to the patient, ensuring they provide specifics before the model commits to an answer.
290.po: In experiments across multiple language models, this framework improves medical question-answering accuracy by an average of 9.48% over baselines, because the system now asks for clarification when it's unclear rather than guessing. The AU-Probe module is lightweight—it doesn't require fine-tuning or multiple passes—making it practical to deploy in real medical settings where speed and safety both matter.

291.bp: In construction and architecture, teams need to exchange information about buildings and projects—what materials to use, what dimensions, what systems go where. There are international standards for this (Industry Foundation Classes, Information Delivery Specification) that make the exchange consistent and machine-readable. But these standards use complex XML formats that are abstract and hard for humans to write by hand.
291.wh: The gap between what humans want to say and what the standard requires is large. A project manager might naturally describe a requirement as 'the structural frame should be steel and support a 200-ton load,' but the standard wants it encoded as a nested XML hierarchy with entity types, property definitions, and numeric codes. Existing tools to bridge this gap have steep learning curves—you have to learn the standard deeply before you can use the tool. This keeps adoption low, and information continues to flow through email and Word documents, which defeats the purpose of having standards.
291.ap: This paper presents SGSS (Schema-Grounded Semantic Structurer), which uses a large language model to translate natural language project requirements directly into valid IDS XML. You type a description in plain English, and the model generates the correct structured output without requiring the user to learn the standard.
291.wh: The model can do this because large language models have absorbed enough examples of XML and domain knowledge (from construction documents on the internet) to internalize the mapping from natural language to structured format. The key is that the model is 'grounded' in the schema—it's constrained to generate only valid XML according to the standard—so it can't hallucinate or invent incorrect structures.
291.po: The result is a significant reduction in the cognitive load of using standards. Construction professionals can now write requirements in their natural language, and the tool handles the translation to standardized format. This increases adoption of information standards in the industry, reducing rework and improving the consistency of information exchange across global teams.

292.bp: Cloud data centers run both interactive services (applications serving users right now) and batch jobs (data processing that can run anytime). To save money and use infrastructure efficiently, operators pack jobs tightly, but this creates contention: if a user-facing service suddenly needs more CPU, a batch job is already using it. The question is: can we adjust resource allocations dynamically so both types of jobs coexist without either starving or wasting resources?
292.wh: Batch jobs in cloud systems vary wildly in how much CPU, memory, and I/O they need during execution—a job that uses 500MB at the start might need 2GB by the end. Predicting this in advance is hard, and once you over-allocate (give it 2GB when it only needs 500MB), you're wasting capacity. Existing autoscaling tools make one-size-fits-all decisions at the cluster level, averaging over many jobs, which means some jobs get too much and others get too little. The tools also require either historical data (which may not exist for new jobs) or predictive models (which add complexity and can be wrong). What you need is a simple method that doesn't require prediction but still adapts to what's actually happening.
292.ap: This paper proposes a two-level vertical pod autoscaler (VPA) strategy that makes decisions at two scales. At the coarse level, it watches cluster-wide utilization trends and recommends resource settings for each job type based on what the cluster is currently experiencing—if memory is scarce, it sets lower memory limits. At the fine level, it watches individual jobs over a sliding window of recent execution and recalibrates what each specific instance of a job actually needs, right now, without waiting for long-term patterns.
292.ww: The reason this works is that coarse adjustments handle the big picture (is memory or CPU the bottleneck today?), while fine adjustments handle the specifics (this particular run of this job is currently using 800MB). By separating these concerns, you avoid both the oversimplification of cluster-wide averaging and the complexity of trying to predict future behavior. The sliding window ensures you respond to what's actually happening in the last few minutes, not what happened last month.
292.po: In production deployment, this two-level strategy increased resource utilization for offline jobs by 8.62% and increased the deployment volume of offline tasks by 41.5%—meaning the cluster can now run many more batch jobs without increasing the number of machines. This directly reduces operational costs while maintaining service quality.

293.bp: Urban traffic is growing unpredictably, and city planners need to forecast traffic flow—how many vehicles will be on a particular road at a particular time—to manage congestion, deploy resources, and design infrastructure. The better the forecast, the more proactive and responsive the city can be.
293.wh: Traffic flow has complex patterns: hourly rhythms (rush hours), daily and weekly cycles (weekday vs weekend), seasonal trends, and sudden disruptions (accidents, weather). Forecasting tools need to capture all of these simultaneously. Many current methods convert traffic time series into images and use computer vision models (which are very effective at finding patterns in pictures), but they freeze the spatial network—they assume the road network is fixed and ignore the geographic and topological structure. Other methods focus on spatial patterns but don't capture temporal rhythms well. The real problem is that traffic is inherently both a spatial structure (how does traffic flow from one road to neighbors?) and a temporal sequence (does today's pattern repeat yesterday's pattern?).
293.ap: This paper proposes MIGC-CMamba, which treats traffic forecasting as a multi-scale problem. First, it converts traffic time series into images at multiple scales (short-term, medium-term, long-term) and applies a vision model to extract patterns that humans recognize in pictures—trends, periodicity, anomalies. Second, it builds a spatial graph not as a fixed network but dynamically using granular-ball clustering—a method that groups roads into meaningful clusters based on their actual traffic behavior, not just geography. Third, it integrates temporal and spatial information adaptively, allowing temporal patterns and spatial relationships to inform each other.
293.ww: The insight is that traffic is easier to forecast when you let vision models see the patterns (they're designed to spot regularities in images) and when you let the spatial structure emerge from data rather than imposing it manually. By converting time series to images at multiple time scales, the model gets to see traffic like a human eye would—as a picture with slopes, peaks, and valleys. By clustering roads dynamically via granular-ball computing, the spatial graph reflects actual traffic dynamics rather than administrative boundaries.
293.po: The result is improved forecast accuracy for traffic flow prediction, which translates to better traffic management in real cities. More accurate forecasts mean better resource allocation (traffic lights, route suggestions, emergency response), less congestion, and more responsive urban mobility.

294.bp: The web is increasingly represented as graphs: social networks (people and their connections), knowledge bases (entities and their relationships), recommendation systems (users, items, and interactions). These graphs often represent very different types of things—users, posts, comments, hashtags, ads—not a uniform network. Algorithms need to learn patterns from these messy, mixed-type networks and make predictions that generalize to new data.
294.wh: The problem is distribution shift. A graph neural network trained on data from 2023 might encounter different patterns in 2024 because user behavior changes, new features appear, or data collection methods shift. The model learned to rely on shortcuts specific to the 2023 data—for example, 'posts with certain tags are mostly from a particular community,' which was true then but isn't universally true. When the distribution shifts, these shortcuts fail. The deeper issue is that in heterogeneous graphs (mixed types of nodes), it's hard to figure out what the stable, generalizable patterns are because you have multiple sources of confusing signals: different node types, different edge types, and different distributions for each combination.
294.ap: This paper proposes InvHG, a framework inspired by causal reasoning. The core idea is to infer hidden environments—subsets of the graph where different rules apply—without being told what those environments are. For example, it might discover that 'posts by celebrity accounts follow one distribution' and 'posts by regular users follow another.' Once these latent environments are identified, the model learns to extract patterns that are stable across environments (invariant representations), not patterns that work well in just one environment. It does this by having multiple expert networks (each specialized for one type of relationship) and learning to fuse their outputs in a way that minimizes the impact of environment-specific shortcuts.
294.ww: The mechanism works because models that explicitly ask 'which parts of my prediction depend on which latent environment?' are forced to separate the stable patterns (things that generalize across environments) from the unstable patterns (shortcuts specific to one environment or one time period). By learning representations that make consistent predictions regardless of which latent environment you're in, the model discovers the causal mechanisms underneath the data rather than just correlations.
294.po: Testing on out-of-distribution (OOD) benchmarks for heterogeneous graphs—where the model is evaluated on data with different distributions than it saw during training—InvHG consistently outperforms existing methods. This means the model makes reliable predictions even when the graph structure or user behavior has shifted, which is critical for real web applications where distribution shifts are inevitable.

295.bp: GPS data from phones and navigation apps creates trajectories—the path a person or vehicle took from A to B. These trajectories are invaluable for urban planning, delivery optimization, traffic analysis, and mobility research. But real-world GPS data is low-quality: it's sampled sparsely (a location point every 5-30 seconds instead of continuously), it has gaps where signal was lost, and points are unevenly distributed. Dense, continuous trajectories are more useful for analysis and decision-making.
295.wh: Reconstructing a trajectory from sparse points is hard because the real path isn't deterministic. A person could have taken a direct route or a scenic detour; a delivery vehicle could have stopped at multiple locations in different orders. Any reconstruction method has to infer what probably happened based on incomplete information, while respecting constraints like 'vehicles can't teleport' and 'paths follow streets.' This is harder than simple interpolation because it's not just connecting the dots—it's inferring the most likely path through a complex space of possible routes, under uncertainty.
295.ap: This paper introduces TRACE, which uses a diffusion model—a type of generative model that starts with pure noise and gradually refines it into real data. TRACE works in reverse: it starts with sparse trajectories (which it treats as corrupted/noisy versions of the true dense trajectory) and gradually denoises them. At each step of denoising, TRACE uses a memory mechanism to keep track of and leverage results from previous steps, ensuring that difficult-to-recover segments (long gaps, turns) are handled better because information from earlier steps is retained.
295.ww: The reason this works is that diffusion models are good at filling in missing information while respecting global structure. By starting with noise and gradually refining, the model learns to generate paths that are smooth, follow realistic movement patterns, and connect sparse points in plausible ways. The memory mechanism ensures that early, high-level decisions (e.g., 'this segment is a highway') inform later, detailed refinements (e.g., 'within the highway segment, the vehicle slowed down here').
295.po: TRACE recovers dense trajectories from sparse GPS data with >26% accuracy improvement over previous methods, without adding significant computational overhead. This directly improves downstream applications: more accurate traffic models, better delivery route optimization, and higher-quality data for urban analytics.

296.bp: In real-world machine learning systems deployed to production, data changes: user behavior shifts, new populations appear, external events alter patterns. A model that worked perfectly on training data can suddenly fail when the input distribution changes. Understanding why this happened—and how to adapt—is essential for keeping systems reliable.
296.wh: The challenge is that data drift is hard to diagnose. Data scientists can run statistical tests to detect drift, but tests don't explain what changed or why. A manager looking at a drop in model performance needs to understand 'is this a seasonal change, a data quality issue, or a shift in user behavior?' Different underlying causes require different remedies. Currently, the process requires deep technical knowledge, manual investigation of data, and conversations with domain experts. It's slow, error-prone, and inaccessible to people without machine learning expertise.
296.ap: This paper presents DriftNavi, a conversational tool powered by large language models that guides users through drift analysis in dialogue. You describe your data and the problem, and DriftNavi asks clarifying questions, runs analyses (drift detection, explanation, adaptation strategies), and explains what it found in language tailored to your background. The tool doesn't require statistical expertise; it's designed to be accessible to practitioners with different levels of technical knowledge.
296.wh: The mechanism works because large language models can maintain context over a conversation, ask questions to disambiguate, and explain technical concepts in multiple ways. By making the tool conversational rather than requiring the user to write code or run commands, DriftNavi lowers the barrier to understanding drift. The underlying analysis (detecting drift, explaining shifts) can be model-free—it doesn't require knowing the original model's weights or architecture.
296.po: The result is a tool that helps practitioners of any background understand and respond to data drift. In case studies on stroke prediction (a high-stakes domain), DriftNavi successfully guides users through detecting drift, understanding its causes, and adapting their model. This extends the maintainability of machine learning systems beyond expert data scientists.

297.bp: Customs agencies worldwide process millions of shipments, and every item needs to be classified—is this a medical device or jewelry? Is this textile or plastic? Classification affects tariffs, regulations, and trade law. Currently, officials manually read descriptions from shippers and classify items, a slow and error-prone task. Automating this could dramatically speed up commerce while improving compliance.
297.wh: The problem is that shippers describe goods in natural language ('blue cotton fabric, 2 meters, decorative pattern') and the classification system expects structured, standardized codes. The descriptions are often in local languages, contain ambiguities, vary widely in format, and may be intentionally vague (to hide value or avoid restrictions). You can't just train a language model on English examples; you need to handle Russian, Chinese, Spanish, and other languages the customs system actually uses. You also need to ensure the model's output is valid—the XML must be properly formatted or it's useless.
297.ap: This paper adapts a sparse mixture-of-experts model (Mixtral-8x7B) to the customs domain using low-rank adaptation (LoRA), which is an efficient fine-tuning method. The model learns to convert unstructured customs descriptions into valid JSON/XML output following the classification standard. To handle the validity problem, they add deterministic post-processing and rule-based validation that corrects malformed outputs. They also use data augmentation—generating additional training examples from a base set—to improve performance on reasoning-oriented classification tasks.
297.ww: The mechanism works because sparse mixture-of-experts models are efficient (they activate only a fraction of their parameters per input, reducing inference costs) and because low-rank adaptation is parameter-efficient (fine-tuning on domain-specific data without updating the entire model). By adding deterministic post-processing, the system can recover from small errors in the model's output—fixing formatting issues without retraining. Data augmentation multiplies the training signal, helping the model learn to reason about customs classifications rather than just memorizing examples.
297.po: On real Russian-language customs declarations, the fine-tuned model produces syntactically valid outputs 98.1% of the time, with post-processing bringing invalid cases down to just 1.06%. Compared to dense model baselines, the sparse mixture-of-experts achieves 10-15 percentage points higher scores on reasoning tasks while maintaining lower inference costs. This directly reduces the manual review burden on customs officers.

298.bp: Video platforms host billions of videos, and some contain harmful content—violence, adult material, hate speech. Platforms are legally and ethically required to detect and remove or restrict this content. But the volume is enormous, and content is continuously uploaded. Detecting issues at scale, quickly, and accurately is a major operational challenge.
298.wh: Current systems often rely on large multimodal models—models that can see images and read text—to analyze each video. These models are accurate but slow: they process videos frame-by-frame, can only be updated monthly or quarterly (retraining is expensive), and don't naturally incorporate feedback from users who report issues or interact with flagged content. They also ignore a wealth of behavioral signals: if many users skip or report a video, that's a signal it might have issues. If an author has a history of uploading problematic content, that's relevant context. Focusing only on the video itself, in isolation, wastes this information.
298.ap: This paper proposes a ranking model for content issue detection that updates daily and incorporates multiple signals. The model takes as input not just the video (via pre-computed embeddings from a multimodal model, computed periodically), but also user behavior features (skips, reports, watch time), video-side signals (views, engagement), and author-side signals (past issues, upload frequency). It uses a cross-order representation fusion architecture to combine these diverse signals. Because it's much simpler than running a full multimodal model on every video, it can be updated daily instead of monthly.
298.wh: The mechanism works because ranking is a simpler task than content understanding. Instead of asking 'is this video harmful?' (which requires semantic understanding), the system asks 'which videos are most likely to have issues based on all available signals?' Multimodal models are still used, but their outputs are cached and updated periodically; the daily ranking model uses those cached features plus behavioral signals to rerank videos. This separation of concerns (semantic understanding done periodically, behavioral signals incorporated daily) reduces computational cost while increasing timeliness.
298.po: A/B testing shows that this daily-updated ranking model achieves higher recall (catches more problematic videos) at the same precision level compared to multimodal baselines. More importantly, online tests demonstrate reduced user exposure to adult content and other issues, contributing to a safer experience. The system is significantly smaller and faster than full multimodal approaches, making it practical to run at platform scale.

299.bp: Graphs appear everywhere: social networks, citation networks, molecular structures, knowledge bases. Clustering—grouping similar things together—is a fundamental task. But graphs have structure at multiple levels: individual nodes (people, papers, atoms) form local neighborhoods, and those neighborhoods cluster into larger components, and those form graph-level patterns. Most clustering methods focus on one level only.
299.wh: The problem is that node-level and graph-level clustering address different structures with different algorithms, and they don't share information. A node clustering method might say 'these 100 nodes form a tight community,' while a graph-level clustering method says 'these clusters actually belong to a higher-order group.' Using both independently wastes information—the local insights could guide the global clustering and vice versa. Also, running two separate models doubles the computation.
299.ap: This paper proposes UGCN (Unified Graph Clustering Network), which performs node-level and graph-level clustering jointly using a dual-branch architecture. One branch extracts node-level features and projects them into distinct cluster layers, creating node prototypes. The other branch captures subgraph embeddings and builds graph-level representations. The branches communicate through contrastive learning: the node-level prototypes guide the subgraph clustering (saying 'nodes in cluster A tend to form similar subgraphs'), while graph-level pseudo-labels provide feedback to refine node clusters (saying 'node clusters that form similar subgraphs are probably correct').
299.wh: The mechanism works because node clustering and graph clustering are complementary: nodes that cluster together often have similar local neighborhoods (node-level structure), and subgraphs that cluster together often contain nodes from the same node clusters (global structure). By making the two branches aware of each other through contrastive objectives, the model forces consistency: if nodes A and B cluster together, their surrounding subgraphs should be similar. This mutual constraint improves both levels of clustering.
299.po: By performing node and graph-level clustering jointly, UGCN achieves better clustering quality at both levels than methods that handle them separately, while using computational resources more efficiently. This is useful for any application that needs to understand graphs at multiple scales—from social network analysis (finding communities and community structures) to knowledge graph curation (identifying related concepts and concept clusters).
